setup.p: Later she finds that the reading at $x = 9$ was logged 5 units too high, so the true value is 12. She corrects it and fits the line again. theory.title: Ridge on Two Columns of Different Size
overview: A model has two features and no intercept. The columns and the target all have mean zero, so an intercept would come out as 0 anyway:

setup.p: with $X = (\mathbf{u}\ \mathbf{v})$. Ridge minimizes $\lVert \mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w} \rVert^2 + \lambda\,(w_u^2 + w_v^2)$, and its weights solve $(X^\top X + \lambda I)\,\mathbf{w} = X^\top \mathbf{y}$. Take $\lambda = 12$.

prompt.p: What is the ridge weight on $\mathbf{u}$?

answer.p: The columns are orthogonal, $\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{v} = 3 - 3 - 3 + 3 = 0$, so $X^\top X$ is diagonal, with the squared lengths $4$ and $36$ on its diagonal, and $X^\top \mathbf{y}$ has entries $\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{y} = 8$ and $\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{y} = 72$.
The system splits into one equation per weight. Least squares gives $8/4 = 2$ and $72/36 = 2$, the same weight on both. Ridge gives

prompt.p: What is the ridge weight on $\mathbf{v}$?

answer.p: Each weight is its least-squares value times $s / (s + \lambda)$, where $s$ is the column's squared length: $4/16 = 1/4$ for $\mathbf{u}$ and $36/48 = 3/4$ for $\mathbf{v}$.

prompt.p: Both features had least-squares weight 2, yet ridge cut one to a quarter and the other to three quarters. Explain why, and say what the shrinkage factors become if $\mathbf{v}$ is first rescaled to the same size as $\mathbf{u}$.

answer.p: The penalty charges $\lambda w^2$ whatever the column, while the fit term charges $s\,(w - 2)^2$, so a column with more spread has more fit to lose and keeps more of its weight. $\mathbf{v}$ is three times larger than $\mathbf{u}$ entry by entry, so its squared length is 9 times larger.

Divide $\mathbf{v}$ by 3, as standardizing would. Its least-squares weight becomes 6, because the same prediction now needs a weight 3 times larger, and its squared length becomes 4. Ridge gives $6 \times 4/16 = 1.5$ on the new column, which is $0.5$ per unit of the old $\mathbf{v}$. Both features are now shrunk by the same factor, $1/4$.

So how much ridge shrinks a feature depends on the unit it was recorded in. Standardizing first puts every feature on the same footing before the penalty is applied, which is why the lesson gives it as the first rule.

theory.title: Three Classes on a Line
overview: A softmax regression sorts a reading $x$ into three classes, A, B and C. Class A is the reference class, with its weights fixed at zero, and the scores are

setup.p: The model predicts the class with the largest probability.

prompt.p: Class A is predicted for every $x$ below some value. What is that value?

answer.p: The softmax is increasing in each score, so the predicted class is the one with the largest score. Compare the scores in pairs:

list: B beats A when $x - 1 > 0$, so for $x > 1$.
C beats A when $2x - 4 > 0$, so for $x > 2$.
C beats B when $2x - 4 > x - 1$, so for $x > 3$.

answer.p: A wins only where it beats both, which is $x < 1$. The crossing of A and C at $x = 2$ is not a boundary of the prediction, because B has the largest score there. So A is predicted for $x < 1$, B for $1 < x < 3$ and C for $x > 3$. In one dimension the regions come in the order of the slopes, 0, 1 and 2.

prompt.p: Now change B's score to $z_B = x + c$ and leave the others alone. Below which value of $c$ is B never predicted?

answer.p: B beats A when $x > -c$ and beats C when $x + c > 2x - 4$, that is $x < c + 4$. B wins on the interval $-c < x < c + 4$, which is empty when $-c \ge c + 4$, that is $c \le -2$.

At $c = -2$ the interval shrinks to the single point $x = 2$, where all three scores are 0 and the classes tie. Below that, A and C share the line and B, with the middle slope, never has the largest score.

prompt.p: With $c = -3$, where does the prediction change from A to C?

answer.p: B never wins, so the boundary is where A and C tie: $2x - 4 = 0$, at $x = 2$. For $x < 2$ the model predicts A and for $x > 2$ it predicts C. B still gets some probability everywhere, largest near $x = 2$, where the softmax gives $e^{-1} / (1 + e^{-1} + 1) \approx 0.16$, but it is never the largest of the three.

overview: A clinic sent a reminder text before some appointments. Of 40 patients who got a reminder, 28 attended. Of 60 who did not, 15 attended. It fits a logistic regression for attendance, $p = \sigma(w_0 + w_1 x)$, with $x = 1$ for a reminder and $x = 0$ otherwise, by maximum likelihood.

prompt.p: What probability of attending does the fitted model give a patient who got a reminder?

answer.p: The model gives every reminded patient the same probability $q_1 = \sigma(w_0 + w_1)$ and every other patient $q_0 = \sigma(w_0)$. So the log-likelihood splits into two groups:

As $w_0$ and $w_1$ range over all numbers, $q_0$ and $q_1$ range over $(0, 1)$ independently, so each bracket can be maximized on its own. Setting the derivative of the first to zero, $28/q_1 - 12/(1 - q_1) = 0$, gives $q_1 = 28/40 = 0.7$. Each group gets its own attendance rate.

prompt.p: What is $w_1$? Give it to three decimal places.

answer.p: The second bracket gives $q_0 = 15/60 = 0.25$. The log-odds are $w_0 = \log(0.25/0.75) = -\ln 3$ and $w_0 + w_1 = \log(0.7/0.3) = \ln(7/3)$, so
$e^{w_1} = 7$ is the odds ratio: the odds of attending are $7/3$ with a reminder and $1/3$ without, seven times larger.

prompt.p: Suppose all 40 reminded patients had attended. What would maximum likelihood do with $w_1$?

answer.p: The first bracket becomes $40 \log q_1$, which keeps rising as $q_1 \to 1$. No finite weights give $q_1 = 1$, so the likelihood has no maximum: the fit pushes $w_0 + w_1$ toward infinity, with $w_0$ still at $-\ln 3$, so $w_1 \to \infty$. Gradient descent would keep growing $w_1$ for as long as it runs. A penalty on $w_1$, or a fixed number of steps, gives a finite answer.

overview: Derive the normal equations, prove the hat matrix is an orthogonal projection, and fit a three-point dataset entirely by hand.

prompt.p: Derive the normal equations $X^\top X \hat{\theta} = X^\top y$ by setting the gradient of the objective to zero.

answer.p: Expand the objective:

answer.tex: \lVert y - X\theta \rVert_2^2 = (y - X\theta)^\top (y - X\theta) = y^\top y - 2 y^\top X \theta + \theta^\top (X^\top X)\theta,

answer.p: using $y^\top X\theta = \theta^\top X^\top y$ (both are scalars, so each equals its own transpose).
Differentiate with the rules from Problem 5, Part 5, noting $X^\top X$ is symmetric:
Setting this to zero gives the normal equations $X^\top X \hat{\theta} = X^\top y$.

This stationary point is a global minimum, not merely a critical point, because the Hessian $2X^\top X$ is positive semidefinite (Problem 5, Part 6), so the objective is convex and Problem 10, Part 1 applies. When $X^\top X$ is invertible the solution is unique, $\hat{\theta} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$.

prompt.p: Prove that $X^\top X$ is invertible if and only if $X$ has full column rank, and describe what happens to the solution set when it does not.

answer.p: The key claim is $\mathcal{N}(X^\top X) = \mathcal{N}(X)$. One inclusion is trivial: $Xz = 0 \Rightarrow X^\top X z = 0$. For the converse, suppose $X^\top X z = 0$. Then

answer.tex: 0 = z^\top X^\top X z = \lVert Xz \rVert_2^2 \ \Longrightarrow \ Xz = 0.

answer.p: So the null spaces coincide. Now $X^\top X$ (which is $d \times d$) is invertible exactly when its null space is trivial, which by the above happens exactly when $\mathcal{N}(X) = \{0\}$. That is, when $X$ has full column rank $d$.

When rank is deficient, the normal equations remain consistent (a solution always exists, since $X^\top y \in \mathcal{C}(X^\top X)$) but the solution set is an entire affine subspace $\hat{\theta} + \mathcal{N}(X)$. Every member gives identical predictions $X\hat\theta$ and identical residuals, so the fit is unique even though the coefficients are not.

This happens whenever $d > N$ or when features are exactly collinear, e.g. including both "height in cm" and "height in m". Near-collinearity is worse in practice than exact collinearity: $X^\top X$ is technically invertible but ill-conditioned, so coefficients become huge and unstable. Ridge regression fixes both cases at once by solving $(X^\top X + \lambda I)\theta = X^\top y$, invertible for any $\lambda > 0$ by the eigenvalue shift of Problem 3, Part 8.

prompt.p: Assume $X$ has full column rank and define the hat matrix $H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top$, so that $\hat{y} = Hy$. Prove that $H$ is symmetric and idempotent ($H^2 = H$), and state what these two properties mean geometrically.

answer.p: Symmetry. Using $(ABC)^\top = C^\top B^\top A^\top$ and the fact that the inverse of a symmetric matrix is symmetric:

answer.tex: H^\top = \big( X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top \big)^\top = X \big((X^\top X)^{-1}\big)^\top X^\top = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top = H.

answer.p: Idempotence. The inner pair cancels:

answer.tex: H^2 = X(X^\top X)^{-1}\underbrace{X^\top X (X^\top X)^{-1}}_{= I}X^\top = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top = H.

answer.p: Together, symmetric plus idempotent means $H$ is the orthogonal projection onto the column space $\mathcal{C}(X)$. Idempotence says projecting twice equals projecting once: once you are in the subspace you stay put. Symmetry says the projection is orthogonal rather than oblique, i.e. it minimizes distance.

Consequences worth knowing: the eigenvalues of $H$ are all $0$ or $1$ (from $\lambda^2 = \lambda$), and $\operatorname{tr}(H) = \operatorname{rank}(H) = d$ counts the effective number of parameters. The residual maker $I - H$ is the complementary projection onto $\mathcal{C}(X)^\perp$, and the diagonal entries $H_{nn}$ are the leverage scores that flag influential observations.

prompt.p: Run the following starter code:

Build the design matrix with an intercept column and solve for $\hat{\theta} = (a, b)$. Explain why $\texttt{np.linalg.solve}$ on the normal equations is preferable to explicitly forming $(X^\top X)^{-1}$, and why $\texttt{np.linalg.lstsq}$ is better still.

lines: theta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)      # -> array([0.3333, 1.5])

answer.p: Why not the explicit inverse. Computing $(X^\top X)^{-1}$ and multiplying costs more arithmetic than a direct solve and is numerically worse: forming an inverse amplifies rounding error, which is then compounded by the subsequent multiplication. The rule of thumb is never to write $\texttt{np.linalg.inv(A) @ b}$ when $\texttt{np.linalg.solve(A, b)}$ will do.

Why lstsq is better still. Forming $X^\top X$ squares the condition number: $\kappa(X^\top X) = \kappa(X)^2$. If $X$ has condition number $10^8$, not unusual with unscaled features, then $X^\top X$ has $10^{16}$, at the edge of double precision, and essentially all significant digits are lost. $\texttt{lstsq}$ works on $X$ directly via QR or SVD, so it only ever sees $\kappa(X)$. It also returns the minimum-norm solution when $X$ is rank deficient, where $\texttt{solve}$ would fail outright with a singular-matrix error.
Both routes give $\hat{\theta} = (1/3, 3/2)$, matching the hand computation in Part 5.

overview: Derive the ridge solution and read it through the SVD, then derive the soft-thresholding rule that makes Lasso coefficients exactly zero.

setup.p: With $X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}^N$, the two regularized problems are

prompt.p: Derive the closed-form ridge solution, and prove that the matrix you must invert is always invertible for $\lambda > 0$, even when $X^\top X$ is singular.

answer.p: Differentiate the objective using the rules of Problem 5, Part 5, noting $\nabla_\theta \lVert\theta\rVert_2^2 = 2\theta$:
which rearranges to $(X^\top X + \lambda I)\hat{\theta} = X^\top y$, so

Invertibility. $X^\top X$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues satisfy $\mu_i \ge 0$. By the eigenvalue-shift result of Problem 3, Part 8, the eigenvalues of $X^\top X + \lambda I$ are $\mu_i + \lambda \ge \lambda > 0$. All eigenvalues are strictly positive, so the matrix is positive definite, hence invertible.

Equivalently, for any $z \ne 0$, $z^\top(X^\top X + \lambda I)z = \lVert Xz\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert z\rVert_2^2 \ge \lambda \lVert z \rVert_2^2 > 0$, so no nonzero vector is in the null space. This is why ridge works when $d > N$: OLS has infinitely many solutions there, ridge has exactly one.

prompt.p: Let $X = U\Sigma V^\top$ be the thin SVD. Express the ridge fitted values $X\hat{\theta}_{\text{ridge}}$ in terms of $U$, $\Sigma$, and $y$, and compare with OLS.

answer.p: Substitute the SVD, and assume for the moment that $X$ has full column rank, so the thin SVD carries square orthogonal $V$ with $V^\top V = I$ and $VV^\top = I$. Then

answer.tex: X^\top X + \lambda I = V\Sigma^2 V^\top + \lambda V V^\top = V\big(\Sigma^2 + \lambda I\big)V^\top,

answer.p: so its inverse is $V(\Sigma^2 + \lambda I)^{-1}V^\top$, and since $X^\top y = V\Sigma U^\top y$,

answer.tex: \hat{\theta}_{\text{ridge}} = V\big(\Sigma^2 + \lambda I\big)^{-1}\Sigma\, U^\top y = \sum_{i} \frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_i^2 + \lambda}\big(u_i^\top y\big) v_i.

answer.p: When $\operatorname{rank}(X) = r < d$ (the $d > N$ case of Part 7), $VV^\top$ is only the projection onto $\mathcal{C}(V)$, so the line above is not literally true. But $X^\top y = V\Sigma U^\top y$ already lies in $\mathcal{C}(V)$, and on that subspace $X^\top X + \lambda I_d$ acts as $V(\Sigma^2 + \lambda I_r)V^\top$ since $(V\Sigma^2V^\top + \lambda I_d)Vc = V(\Sigma^2 + \lambda I_r)c$, so the same formula for $\hat{\theta}_{\text{ridge}}$ still follows.
Multiplying by $X = U\Sigma V^\top$ gives the fitted values

answer.tex: X\hat{\theta}_{\text{ridge}} = \sum_{i} \frac{\sigma_i^2}{\sigma_i^2 + \lambda}\big(u_i^\top y\big)\, u_i, \qquad \text{versus} \qquad X\hat{\theta}_{\text{OLS}} = \sum_i \big(u_i^\top y\big) u_i.

answer.p: So ridge keeps the same directions $u_i$ but multiplies each by a shrinkage factor $\sigma_i^2/(\sigma_i^2 + \lambda) \in (0, 1)$. The shrinkage is direction-dependent and this is the whole story:

list: Where $\sigma_i^2 \gg \lambda$ the factor is near $1$: high-variance, well-determined directions pass through nearly untouched.
Where $\sigma_i^2 \ll \lambda$ the factor is near $0$: the noisy, poorly-determined directions are crushed.

answer.p: OLS divides by $\sigma_i$, so a tiny singular value produces an enormous coefficient driven entirely by noise. Ridge replaces $1/\sigma_i$ with $\sigma_i/(\sigma_i^2 + \lambda)$, which stays bounded by $1/(2\sqrt{\lambda})$. No factor is ever exactly zero, which is precisely why ridge shrinks but never selects.

prompt.p: Assume $X$ has orthonormal columns, so $X^\top X = I$, and let $z = X^\top y$ be the OLS solution.
Derive the Lasso solution coordinate by coordinate, and show that it is exactly zero whenever $\lvert z_j \rvert \le \lambda$.

answer.p: With $X^\top X = I$, expand the squared-error term:

answer.tex: \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert y - X\theta\rVert_2^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert y \rVert^2 - \theta^\top X^\top y + \tfrac{1}{2}\theta^\top \theta = \text{const} + \sum_j \left( \tfrac{1}{2}\theta_j^2 - \theta_j z_j \right).

answer.p: The $\ell_1$ penalty is also separable, so the whole objective decouples into $d$ independent scalar problems:
Case $\theta_j > 0$: $g'(\theta_j) = \theta_j - z_j + \lambda = 0$ gives $\theta_j = z_j - \lambda$, which is consistent with $\theta_j > 0$ only if $z_j > \lambda$.
Case $\theta_j < 0$: $g'(\theta_j) = \theta_j - z_j - \lambda = 0$ gives $\theta_j = z_j + \lambda$, consistent only if $z_j < -\lambda$.

Case $\theta_j = 0$: here $\lvert\theta_j\rvert$ is not differentiable, so use the subdifferential $\partial\lvert\theta_j\rvert = [-1, 1]$ at $0$. Optimality requires $0 \in \{-z_j + \lambda s : s \in [-1,1]\}$, i.e. $z_j = \lambda s$ for some $s \in [-1,1]$, which holds exactly when $\lvert z_j \rvert \le \lambda$.
Combining the three cases gives the soft-thresholding operator

This is the proof that Lasso produces exact zeros. The kink in $\lvert\theta\rvert$ at the origin means the penalty's slope does not vanish as $\theta \to 0$, it stays at $\pm\lambda$, so it can hold a coefficient pinned at zero against a data pull of up to $\lambda$. Ridge's penalty $\theta^2$ has derivative $2\theta \to 0$, which can never overcome a nonzero data term. The corresponding ridge solution here is $\hat{\theta}_j = z_j/(1+\lambda)$: every coefficient shrunk by the same ratio, none of them zero.

prompt.p: Consider two regularized linear regression models trained on the same dataset. Model A uses $\ell_1$-regularization, and Model B uses $\ell_2$-regularization. Both use the same regularization strength $\lambda > 0$. Which statement is most likely true?

choices: A. Models A and B have the same number of non-zero weights.
B. Model A has fewer non-zero weights than Model B.
C. Model B has fewer non-zero weights than Model A.
D. Neither model can produce zero weights.
E. There is no way to know which model has fewer non-zero weights.

answer.p: By Part 3, $\ell_1$ sets a coefficient to exactly zero whenever the data signal for it is below $\lambda$, while $\ell_2$ shrinks every coefficient by the factor $1/(1+\lambda)$ and produces exact zeros only in the measure-zero case $z_j = 0$. So Model A (Lasso) has fewer non-zero weights.

The geometric picture says the same thing. Both problems can be written as minimizing the squared error subject to a budget on $\theta$. The $\ell_1$ budget region is a cross-polytope with vertices on the coordinate axes, and the elliptical error contours typically first touch it at a vertex. At a vertex, some coordinates are exactly zero. The $\ell_2$ region is a smooth ball with no corners, so the contact point almost never has a zero coordinate.

answer.result: B. Model A has fewer non-zero weights than Model B.

prompt.p: Explain why, before fitting either regularized model, you should (a) standardize the features and (b) leave the intercept out of the penalty.

answer.p: (a) Standardize. The penalties $\lVert\theta\rVert_2^2$ and $\lVert\theta\rVert_1$ treat all coefficients on one scale, but coefficients carry the inverse units of their features. Measuring a length in metres rather than millimetres multiplies its coefficient by $1000$ and thus its penalty contribution by $10^6$ for ridge. The model would then be penalized for an arbitrary choice of units, effectively regularizing large-scale features into oblivion. Standardizing each column to zero mean and unit variance makes the penalty scale-invariant and the single shared $\lambda$ meaningful.

(b) Do not penalize the intercept. The intercept sets the overall level of the predictions, and shrinking it toward zero would bias predictions toward zero, which is meaningless unless zero happens to be a special value of $y$. Concretely, if you added a constant $c$ to every $y_n$, an unpenalized intercept would simply absorb it and leave the slopes unchanged. A penalized intercept would not, so the fit would depend on where you happened to put the origin.

The standard implementation centres $X$ and $y$, fits the penalized slopes on the centered data, and recovers $\hat{a} = \bar{y} - \hat{b}^\top \bar{x}$ afterwards. Standardization must be fitted on the training fold only: computing means and standard deviations over the full dataset before splitting leaks test information, a point Problem 14, Part 5 returns to.

prompt.p: Ridge regression is a biased estimator, while OLS is unbiased. Explain why one would ever prefer the biased estimator.

answer.p: Because prediction error depends on bias *and* variance, and OLS can have enormous variance. Squared error decomposes as $\text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \sigma^2$ (derived in Problem 14, Part 1), and minimizing it does not mean driving bias to zero.

Part 2 makes the trade explicit. In a direction with a tiny singular value $\sigma_i$, the OLS coefficient is $(u_i^\top y)/\sigma_i$: since $u_i^\top y$ contains noise of standard deviation $\sigma$, that coefficient has standard deviation $\sigma/\sigma_i$, which blows up. Ridge multiplies it by $\sigma_i^2/(\sigma_i^2 + \lambda)$, accepting a small bias in exchange for a large variance reduction in exactly the directions where the data are least informative.

There is a theoretical guarantee behind this: for every $X$, $y$ and noise variance $\sigma^2 > 0$ there exists some $\lambda > 0$ whose ridge estimator has strictly smaller expected squared error than OLS. The gain is largest when features are collinear or $d$ is comparable to $N$, and negligible when $N \gg d$ with well-conditioned features. Since the optimal $\lambda$ depends on unknown quantities, it is chosen by cross-validation.

prompt.p: Write code computing $\hat{\theta}_{\text{ridge}}$, and explain why the $d \times d$ formula of Part 1 is the wrong one to use here.

lines: # Dual form: solve the N x N system instead of the d x d one.
theta_ridge = X.T @ np.linalg.solve(X @ X.T + lam * np.eye(X.shape[0]), y)

answer.p: The identity being used is

which can be verified by multiplying both sides by $(X^\top X + \lambda I_d)$ on the left and $(XX^\top + \lambda I_N)$ on the right: both reduce to $X^\top(XX^\top + \lambda I_N) = (X^\top X + \lambda I_d)X^\top$, which is true since both equal $X^\top X X^\top + \lambda X^\top$.

Why it matters here: $d = 200$ and $N = 50$, so the primal form inverts a $200 \times 200$ matrix while the dual inverts a $50 \times 50$ one, which is $64\times$ less work at cubic cost. In the regime $d \gg N$ that gap is the difference between feasible and not, and this dual form is exactly the door to kernel ridge regression, since $XX^\top$ is a Gram matrix of inner products that can be replaced by a kernel.

Running it, $\hat{\theta}_{\text{ridge}}$ recovers large values on the first five coordinates and small but strictly nonzero values elsewhere, which is the shrink-everything behavior of Part 2. Lasso on the same data would zero out most of the $195$ irrelevant coordinates outright.

theory.title: Logistic Regression, Log-Odds, and Convexity
overview: Derive the gradient and Hessian of logistic regression, prove the loss is convex, and show why perfectly separable data has no solution.

setup.p: Given $X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$ and labels $y_n \in \{0, 1\}$, logistic regression models
The negative log-likelihood (equivalently, the binary cross-entropy loss) is

prompt.p: Prove that the model is equivalent to asserting that the log-odds are linear:

answer.p: Write $t = \theta^\top X[n]$, so $p = \sigma(t) = 1/(1 + e^{-t})$. Then
so the odds ratio is
Taking logarithms gives $\log\frac{p}{1-p} = t = \theta^\top X[n]$, as claimed. The map $p \mapsto \log\frac{p}{1-p}$ is the logit, and it is exactly $\sigma^{-1}$.

This is what makes coefficients interpretable: increasing feature $j$ by one unit adds $\theta_j$ to the log-odds, i.e. multiplies the odds by $e^{\theta_j}$, regardless of the other features. It is also the reason the model is called *linear* even though the output is manifestly nonlinear in the inputs: linearity lives on the log-odds scale.

prompt.p: Derive $\nabla_\theta L$ and express it in matrix form.

answer.p: Let $t_n = \theta^\top X[n]$ so $p_n = \sigma(t_n)$. First simplify the per-example loss by substituting $\log p_n = \log\sigma(t_n)$ and $\log(1 - p_n)$, then differentiate through $t_n$.
By Problem 5, Part 2, $\frac{\partial p_n}{\partial t_n} = p_n(1 - p_n)$, and $\frac{\partial t_n}{\partial \theta_j} = X_{nj}$. The derivative of the $n$-th term with respect to $p_n$ is
Multiply by $\partial p_n / \partial t_n = p_n(1-p_n)$ and watch the cancellation:

answer.tex: \frac{\partial L_n}{\partial t_n} = \left( -\frac{y_n}{p_n} + \frac{1-y_n}{1-p_n} \right) p_n(1-p_n) = -y_n(1 - p_n) + (1 - y_n)p_n = p_n - y_n.

answer.p: Then by the chain rule through $t_n$,

This is the same "predicted minus actual" structure found in Problem 6, Part 3 for softmax, and for the same reason: the logarithm in the loss inverts the exponential in the link function. Note the striking similarity to the least-squares gradient $-\frac{2}{N}X^\top(y - X\theta)$: the only change is that the raw prediction $X\theta$ is replaced by $\sigma(X\theta)$. Both are instances of the general exponential-family result $\nabla L = X^\top(\text{prediction} - \text{target})$.

prompt.p: Compute the Hessian $\nabla^2_\theta L$ and prove that $L$ is convex.

answer.p: Differentiate the gradient again. Since $\frac{\partial p_n}{\partial \theta_k} = p_n(1-p_n)X_{nk}$,

answer.tex: \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial\theta_j \partial\theta_k} = \sum_{n} X_{nj}\, \frac{\partial p_n}{\partial \theta_k} = \sum_n p_n(1 - p_n) X_{nj}X_{nk},

answer.p: which in matrix form is

answer.tex: \nabla^2_\theta L = X^\top D X, \qquad D = \operatorname{diag}\big( p_0(1-p_0), \dots, p_{N-1}(1-p_{N-1}) \big).

answer.p: Convexity. For any $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$, writing $w = Xz$,

answer.tex: z^\top X^\top D X z = w^\top D w = \sum_n p_n(1 - p_n)\, w_n^2 \ \ge \ 0,

answer.p: because each $p_n \in (0,1)$ makes $p_n(1-p_n) > 0$. The Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere, so by Problem 10, Part 2 the loss is convex, and by Problem 10, Part 1 any local minimum is global.

Two caveats. The Hessian depends on $\theta$ through $D$ (unlike least squares, where it is constant), which is why there is no closed-form solution: setting $\nabla L = 0$ gives $X^\top\sigma(X\theta) = X^\top y$, transcendental in $\theta$. And $L$ is strictly convex only if $X$ has full column rank. Otherwise there are flat directions, which is one route to the non-existence problem in Part 4.

prompt.p: Call the data linearly separable if there exists $\theta_0$ with $\theta_0^\top X[n] > 0$ whenever $y_n = 1$ and $\theta_0^\top X[n] < 0$ whenever $y_n = 0$.
Prove that in this case the maximum likelihood estimate does not exist, and state the standard fix.

answer.p: Consider the scaled parameter $\theta = c\,\theta_0$ for $c > 0$, and examine each term of the loss.

If $y_n = 1$, then $t_n = c\,\theta_0^\top X[n] \to +\infty$ as $c \to \infty$, so $p_n = \sigma(t_n) \to 1$ and $-\log p_n \to 0$. If $y_n = 0$, then $t_n \to -\infty$, so $p_n \to 0$ and $-\log(1 - p_n) \to 0$. Therefore

Since $L > 0$ strictly for every finite $\theta$ (each $p_n$ lies strictly in $(0,1)$, so every term is strictly positive), the infimum $0$ is approached but never attained. The optimizer therefore drives $\lVert\theta\rVert \to \infty$ and no maximum likelihood estimate exists.

In practice you see the loss decreasing toward zero while the weights grow without bound, the sigmoid saturates, the Hessian entries $p_n(1-p_n) \to 0$, and gradients underflow. The fitted probabilities become $0$ or $1$. They are perfectly confident and perfectly uncalibrated.

The fix is regularization: minimizing $L(\theta) + \lambda\lVert\theta\rVert_2^2$ makes the objective coercive (it tends to $+\infty$ as $\lVert\theta\rVert \to \infty$) and strictly convex, so a unique finite minimizer always exists. Among the infinitely many separating hyperplanes, the penalty selects the one with the smallest norm, which is close to the maximum-margin choice made by an SVM. Separability is common precisely when $d \ge N$, so this is the normal case in high dimensions, not an exotic one.

prompt.p: A fitted logistic regression predicting loan default has coefficient $\theta_j = 0.7$ for a feature measured in standardized units. Which interpretation is correct?

choices: A. A one-unit increase in feature $j$ raises the probability of default by $0.7$.
B. A one-unit increase in feature $j$ raises the probability of default by $70\%$.
C. A one-unit increase in feature $j$ multiplies the odds of default by $e^{0.7} \approx 2.01$.
D. A one-unit increase in feature $j$ multiplies the probability of default by $0.7$.
E. Feature $j$ accounts for $70\%$ of the model's predictions.

answer.p: By Part 1 the model is linear in the log-odds, so adding one unit to feature $j$ adds $\theta_j$ to the log-odds and therefore multiplies the odds by $e^{\theta_j} = e^{0.7} \approx 2.01$.

A, B, and D are wrong because the effect on the *probability* is not constant: it depends on where you start. The derivative $\partial p/\partial x_j = \theta_j\, p(1-p)$ is largest at $p = 0.5$ (giving $0.7 \times 0.25 = 0.175$) and nearly zero when $p$ is close to $0$ or $1$. Moving someone from $p = 0.5$ to $p \approx 0.67$ is a large change. Moving someone from $p = 0.99$ barely moves them at all.
This constant-effect-on-odds property is exactly what the logit link buys, and it is why odds ratios are the standard reporting unit for logistic models.

answer.result: C. The odds are multiplied by $e^{0.7} \approx 2.01$.

parts.requirement: Do not use scipy. Your implementation must not overflow or produce nan for large-magnitude inputs.

prompt.p: Run the following starter code:
Explain what goes wrong in the direct implementation below, and write a stable version.

answer.p: Two failures. For $t = -800$, $\texttt{np.exp(800)}$ overflows to $\texttt{inf}$ inside the sigmoid, and for $t = 800$ the sigmoid rounds to exactly $1.0$, so $\log(1 - p) = \log 0 = -\infty$. Multiplying $-\infty$ by a zero coefficient then gives $\texttt{nan}$, so even examples whose term should not matter poison the total.
The stable route rewrites the loss in terms of $t$ directly. Substituting $p = \sigma(t)$ into the per-example loss and simplifying gives

answer.tex: L_n = \log\big(1 + e^{t_n}\big) - y_n t_n = \max(t_n, 0) + \log\big(1 + e^{-\lvert t_n \rvert}\big) - y_n t_n.

answer.p: The identity is the log-sum-exp trick applied to $\log(1 + e^t)$: factoring out $e^{\max(t,0)}$ leaves an exponential of $-\lvert t\rvert \le 0$, which can only underflow harmlessly toward $0$, never overflow. $\texttt{np.log1p}$ then computes $\log(1 + x)$ accurately for tiny $x$, where $\texttt{np.log(1 + x)}$ would lose all precision to rounding.

This is why frameworks expose $\texttt{binary\_cross\_entropy\_with\_logits}$ rather than asking you to apply a sigmoid first: passing raw logits lets the library use this formulation, whereas passing probabilities has already destroyed the information needed for it.
